The Effect of Nitrogen on the Localized
Corrosion Resistance of Duplex
Stainless Steel Simulated Weldments
H. TSUGE, Y. TARUTANI, and T. KUDO*
Abstract
The effect of nitrogen, which is one of the most important elements in duplex stainless steels (SSs), was
investigated for resistance to pitting corrosion and stress corrosion cracking (SCC) in various
environments. The increase in nitrogen content increases the resistance of the base metal, which
results from the improvement in the resistance of the γ-phase, which has lower chromium and
molybdenum contents compared to α-phase. Nitrogen is an important element in sustaining the
corrosion resistance of the heat affected zone (HAZ), which is heated to 1350 C or higher, because
nitrogen promotes the formation of γ-phase during the cooling process after welding and avoids the
precipitation of chromium carbides or nitrides at grain boundaries. When the nitrogen content is less
than 0.08% in 22%Cr, 5.5%Ni, and 3%Mo base composition, the HAZ has little γ-phase to lead to the
high susceptibility to intergranular corrosion and intergranular stress corrosion cracking (IGSCC) occurs
even in a pure
environment containing no
Nitrogen has little effect on the precipitation
behavior of the other phase in the base metal during aging heat treatment of around 700 C.
Introduction
The recent search for new sources of hydrocarbons has led to the
production from more severe environments. Such wells are deep and
often constructed at offshore sites. The environments usually contain
considerable amounts of carbon dioxide
( \mathsf { C O } _ { 2 } ) ,
hydrogen sulfide
(HS), and concentrated brine. Oil and gas production from these
wells expose construction materials, such as tubulars and line pipes,
to very severe corrosive conditions.
Low alloy steels are not suitable because inhibited systems are
not desirable for offshore use or for the high temperature portion of
the well. The corrosion resistance of highly alloyed materials, for
example, duplex stainless steels (SSs), high nickel SSs, and
nickel-base alloys have been evaluated for the purpose of selecting
proper materials depending on the various well condition.1-6Among
those highly alloyed materials, 22%Cr duplex SS line pipes have
been widely used in the field that contains
{ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }

small amounts of H₂S. Duplex SSs usually contain some amount of

joints. Corrosion behaviors such as pitting, intergranular corrosion,

researchers.7,8 The effect of nitrogen on corrosion behavior, how-
ever, has not been clarified yet.
In this paper, the effect of nitrogen content on the corrosion
resistance of 22%Cr duplex SSs was investigated with respect to the
base metals, the low temperature HAZ, and the high temperature
HAZ, which is heated to 1350 C or higher.

Test Method
The pitting potential was measured potentiodynamically in 5%
NaCl deaerated solution at 60 C at a sweep rate of 20 mV/min with
a potentiostat. The (reference) SCE and the platinum counter
electrode were used in this study. The test specimen, a disk 15 mm
in diameter and 2 mm in thickness, was polished with No. 600 emery
paper, washed with water and alcohol, and then degreased with
acetone. The potential at which the anodic current density increases
dramatically by the occurrence of pitting was adopted as the pitting
potential (Vc’).

Figure 5 shows the typical example of microstructure of the
base metal and the HAZ(B) with different nitrogen contents. In the

Corrosion Resistance of High Temperature HAZ
In order to investigate the effect of nitrogen content on the
corrosion behavior of the high temperature HAZ, i.e., HAZ(B) in
Figure 4, the materials were heated with the simulated heat pattern
shown in Figure 2. Figure 15 shows the effect of peak temperature at
heat cycle on SCC susceptibility of 22%Cr duplex SS containing
0.14% nitrogen. SCC occurs only at the peak temperature of 1375 C.
That microstructure with various peak temperatures is shown in
Figure 16. The duplex phase transforms to single α-phase when the
peak temperature exceeds 1350 C and then needle-shaped γ-phase
precipitates during the cooling process. Therefore, the peak temper-

It has been shown that nitrogen is beneficial in improving the
pitting corrosion resistance of the base metal. This beneficial effect of
nitrogen can be attributed to improving the pitting corrosion resistant
of the austenite phase, as discussed below. Chromium and molyb-
denum contents in the ferrite and austenite phases are almost
constant independent of nitrogen content, as shown in Figure 21. The
austenite phase has ~21%Cr-2.5%Mo, while the ferrite phase has
23%Cr-3.5%Mo. Assuming that the pitting index equation is
\complement \pm
3Mo + 16N (as proposed in Reference 9) and that the nitrogen exists
only in the austenite phase of 60%, as shown in Figure 1, the nitrogen
content required to get the same pitting corrosion resistance in
austenite phase as that in the ferrite phase is ~0.18%. Therefore, the
pitting corrosion is thought to initiate at the austenite phase below the
nítrogen content of 0.18% from this rough estimation. Figure 22
shows the microscopic observation of pitting initiation of the 22%Cr
duplex SS in NaCi solution. In the alloys with nitrogen contents of
pitting corrosion is observed to initiate in austenite phase.
When the nitrogen content increases to 0.164%, it can be seen that
pitting occurs at random on the ferrite and austenite phases. The
estimation mentioned above almost agrees with the observation.

Conclusion
The effects of nitrogen content of 22%Cr duplex SS on the
corrosion resistance of welds was investigated. The results obtained
are as follows:
1. The increase in nitrogen content increases the resistance to
pitting corrosion and SCC of the base metal, which results from the
improvement in the resistance of austenite phase by the dissolved
nitrogen itself.
2. Nitrogen has little effect on the intergranular corrosion at the
low temperature HAZ in the Huey test
3. More than 0.12% nitrogen is required for the 22%Cr, 5.5%Ni,
and 3%Mo base alloys to maintain the corrosion resistance at high
temperature HAZ, which is heated to 1350 C or higher. When the
nitrogen content is less than 0.077%, the HAZ, which contains little
austenite phase, has the high susceptibility to intergranular corrosion
and IGSCC.

Influence of Grain Boundary
Microstructure on the Susceptibility
of Alloy 600 to Intergranular Attack
and Stress Corrosion Cracking
S. M. PAYNE* and P. McINTYRE**
Abstract
The influence of grain boundary microstructure on the susceptibility of thermally treated (TT) Inconel
Alloy 600 to intergranular attack (IGA) and stress corrosion cracking (SCC) in 30%NaOH +
at 350 C was investigated. Both mill-annealed (MA) and laboratory solution-annealed
alloys were aged at 700 C to establish the effect of initial processing on the material's response to
thermal treatment. Treatments of 1 h or more at 700 C greatly improved the SCC resistance of
solution-annealed material but did not improve the performance of MA material containing a high density
of intragranular carbides. The poor behavior of this material after thermal treatment was associated with
the formation of small
carbides qrowing at a high angle to the boundaries and the development
of these into cellular colonies. This is attributed to the use of a MA temperature that was too low to take
into solution sufficient carbon for the development of semicontinuous grain boundary carbides during
the subsequent TT process.
Introduction
Mill-annealed (MA) Inconel Alloy 600, an austenitic nickel-based
alloy, has been widely used for the manufacture of pressurized water
reactor (PWR) steam-generator tubing since 1967.1 However, a
combination of intergranular attack (IGA) and stress corrosion
cracking (SCC) has occurred at the outer surfaces of the tubes in
some steam generators where caustic impurities from the secondary
water have concentrated in crevices between the tubes and adjacent
tube sheets or support plates.²
In recent years, thermal treatment (TT) after final MA has been
used to improve the resistance of Alloy 600 to SCC in caustic
environments.1 This treatment, at ~700 C for ~15 to 20 h, causes
chromium carbides to precipitate at the grain boundaries and allows
rehomogenization of the chromium content in the vicinity of most
boundaries. It also reduces residual stresses and the effects of cold
work introduced during the tubing manufacture. TT has been
reported³ to significantly improve resistance to SCC for Alloy 600 with
carbon contents in the range of 0.006 to 0.046% by weight. The
